label: main
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: Reimannth
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Reimannth}
Let $\mathbf{v}:[0,T]\times\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be a continuous vector field, such that for each $t$ one has
$$\limsup_{|z|\to+\infty}\frac{|\mathbf{v}(t,z)|}{|z|\,\log|z|}<+\infty.$$
Suppose that the distributional derivatives $\partial \mathbf{v}(t,\cdot)$ and $\overline\partial \mathbf{v}(t,\cdot)$ are locally integrable functions of $z\in\mathbb C$, and moreover suppose that 
$$\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|\overline\partial\mathbf{v} (t,\cdot)\|_\infty \leq C_0<\infty.$$
Then, $\mathbf{v}$ admits a unique flow $X(t,z)$ of $K_t$-quasiconformal maps $X(t,\cdot):\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$, and
$$K_t\leq \exp \left(2\int_0^t \|\overline\partial \mathbf{v}(s,\cdot)\|_\infty \,ds\right).$$
head: environment

label: LinftyK
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us consider a real number $R>0$. For each such $R$ and given any two arbitrary points $x$ and $y$ in the plane, we can always divide the plane into two regions, $|x-y|\leq R$ and $|x-y|>R$. Therefore,
$$\aligned
|K\ast f(x)|
&\leq\int_{\mathbb C}|K(x-y)\,f(y)|\,dA(y)\\
&=\int_{|x-y|\leq R}|K(x-y)\,f(y)|\,dA(y)+\int_{|x-y|>R}|K(x-y)\,f(y)|\,dA(y)\\
&\leq\|f\|_\infty\,\int_{|x-y|\leq R}\frac{C}{|x-y|}\,dA(y)+\frac{C}{R}\int_{|x-y|>R}|f(y)|dy\\
&\leq CR\,\|f\|_{\infty}+\frac{C}{R}\|f\|_1
\endaligned$$ 
If we minimize the term on the right hand of the inequality as a function of $R$, the best possible value attainable is $R=\|f\|_1^\frac12\,\|f\|_\infty^{-\frac12}.$ This gives the bound \eqref{without support}. The bound \eqref{with support} is an immediate consequence of \eqref{without support}. Concerning (c), let us assume that $diam(\operatorname{supp}(f))=2R$. It is not restrictive to assume $0\in\operatorname{supp}(f)$, so that $\operatorname{supp}(f)\subset \overline{D(0,R)}$. Then, at points $x$ such that $|x|>2R$ one has
$$\aligned
|K\ast f(x)|
&\leq C\int_{|y-x|\leq R}\frac{|f(y-x)|}{|y|}\,dA(y)\\ 
&\leq C\|f\|_\infty\,\int_{|y-x|\leq R}\frac{1}{|y|}\,dA(y)\\ 
&\leq C\|f\|_\infty\,\frac{R^2}{|x|-R}\leq C\,\frac{\|f\|_\infty\,\text{diam}(\operatorname{supp}(f))^2}{|x|}, \\ 
\endaligned$$
as claimed.
head: environment

label: qcflows
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The structure of the Cauchy Kernel makes it clear that
$$2\|\overline\partial{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}}^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_\infty=  \|\omega^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_\infty=\|\omega^\epsilon_0\|_\infty\leq\|\omega_0\|_\infty.$$
Moreover, from Lemma \ref{LinftyK} (c) we know that $\operatorname{\textbf{v}}^{\epsilon}(t,\cdot)$ vanishes at $\infty$ like $\frac{C}{|z|}$. Therefore,
$$\aligned
\underset{|z|\to\infty}{\limsup}\frac{|\operatorname{\textbf{v}}^{\epsilon}(t,z)|}{|z|\log\left(e+|z|\right)}&\leq C<+\infty.
\endaligned$$
Thus, all the requirements in Reimann's Theorem \ref{Reimannth} are fulfilled, and quasiconformality follows, with quasiconformality constant 
$$\mathcal{K}_t\leq \exp\left(2\int_0^t\|\overline\partial \operatorname{\textbf{v}}^\epsilon(s,\cdot)\|_\infty ds\right)\leq e^{t\|\omega_0\|_\infty}$$
and by definition, $\mathcal{K}_t\geq1$. Therefore, part (a) is clear. Part (b)  says that quasiconformal maps are quantitatively quasisymmetric. The interested reader should check \cite[Corollary 3.10.4]{AIM} for a detailed proof. Part (c) follows from \cite[Theorem 13.1.5]{AIM} and the classical area distortion estimates for $\mathcal{K}_t$-quasiconformal maps.
head: environment

label: compactness
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To prove the claim (a), let us remind from Lemma \ref{qcflows} that $X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)$ is quasisymmetric. That is, given any three points $z_0,z,w\in\mathbb C$ we have
$$
\frac{|X^\epsilon(t,z )-X^\epsilon(t,z_0)|}{|X^\epsilon(t,w)-X^\epsilon(t,z_0)|}\leq \eta_{\mathcal{K}_t}\left(\frac{|z -z_0|}{|w-z_0|}\right).
$$
As a consequence
$$\aligned
 |X^\epsilon(t,z )-X^\epsilon(t,z_0)| 
 &\leq \eta_{\mathcal{K}_t}(|z-z_0|/|w-z_0|) |X^\epsilon(t,w)-X^\epsilon(t,z_0)|\\
 &\leq \eta_{\mathcal{K}_t}(|z-z_0|/|w-z_0|) (|X^\epsilon(t,w)|+|X^\epsilon(t,z_0)|)\\
 &\leq \eta_{\mathcal{K}_t}(|z-z_0|/|w-z_0|) ( C(t,|w|) +C(t,|z_0|))
\endaligned$$
In particular, by leaving $w$ fixed one can easily get that $X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)$ is equicontinuous at $z_0$. \\
The family of maps, $\{X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\}_\epsilon$ is pointwise equicontinuous and locally uniformly bounded. Therefore, Arzela-Ascoli theorem ensures the existence of a locally uniform accumulation point $X(t,\cdot)$. It is worth mentioning that by classical tools in \emph{Geometric Function Theory} \cite[Theorem 3.1.3]{AIS} it can only be either $\mathcal{K}_t$-quasiconformal or constant. To see that it cannot be constant, one must observe that the quasisymmetry bounds are preserved by uniform limits. Being two sided, these quasisymmetry bounds guarantee bijectivity. Therefore, the accumulation point $X(t,\cdot)$ is $\mathcal{K}_t$-quasiconformal.
head: environment

label: support
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{support}
Let $X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)$ be as before, and assume that $\omega_0^\epsilon$ has compact support. Then 
$$\omega^\epsilon_0(z)=0\hspace{1cm}\Longrightarrow\hspace{1cm} \overline\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)=0,$$
in other words $X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)$ is conformal outside of $\operatorname{supp}\omega_0^\epsilon$.
head: environment

label: pointw
title: Proof
body_md:
The $\mathcal{K}_t$-quasiconformality of $X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)$ ensures the existence of a well-defined, uniformly elliptic Beltrami coefficient $\mu^\epsilon(t,\cdot)=\frac{\overline\partial X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)}{\partial X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)}$, and moreover we know that 
$$\|\mu^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_\infty\leq\frac{\mathcal{K}_t-1}{\mathcal{K}_t+1}.$$
The smoothness in time of $\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)$ and $\overline\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)$ guarantees that $t\mapsto \mu^\epsilon(t,z)$ is also smooth. From the equation for the flow $\dot{X^\epsilon}(t,z)=\operatorname{\textbf{v}}^\epsilon(t,X^\epsilon(t,z))$ and the chain rule we get that
$$\aligned
\overline\partial \operatorname{\textbf{v}}^\epsilon(t,X^\epsilon(t,z))
&=\frac{\frac{d}{dt}\overline\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)\,\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)-\overline\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)\,\frac{d}{dt}\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)}{J^\epsilon(t,z)}\\
&=\frac{\frac{d}{dt}\mu^\epsilon(t,z)\,\left(\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)\right)^2}{J^\epsilon(t,z)}\\
&=\frac{\frac{d}{dt}\mu^\epsilon(t,z)}{1-|\mu^\epsilon(t,z)|^2}\,\frac{\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)}{\overline{\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)}}\\
\endaligned$$
On the other hand, from the kernel structure we have
$$
2|\overline\partial \operatorname{\textbf{v}}^\epsilon(t,X^\epsilon(t,z))|= |\omega^\epsilon(t,X^\epsilon(t,z))|=|\omega^\epsilon_0(z)|.
$$
Thus
$$
\aligned
\frac{ \frac{d}{dt}|\mu^\epsilon(t,z)|}{1-|\mu^\epsilon(t,z)|^2}
&\leq\frac{\left|\frac{d}{dt}\mu^\epsilon(t,z)\right|}{1-|\mu^\epsilon(t,z)|^2}=\frac12\,|\omega^\epsilon_0(z)|
\endaligned$$
Now, given any time $t>0$, we can integrate on $(0,t)$ the above inequality to obtain that
\begin{equation}\label{pointw}
\log\left(\frac{1+|\mu^\epsilon(t,z)|}{1-|\mu^\epsilon(t,z)|}\right)\leq t\,|\omega^\epsilon_0(z)|,
\end{equation}
since $X^\epsilon(0,z)=z$ implies $\mu^\epsilon(0,z)=0$. Now, if $\omega^\epsilon_0(z)=0$ then necessarily $\mu^\epsilon(t,z)=0$ and hence $\overline\partial X^\epsilon(t,z)=0$. The claim follows.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The above proof also shows that, at time $t=0$,
$$\frac{\omega^{\epsilon}_{0}(z)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\,\omega^\epsilon(0,\cdot)(z)=\overline\partial \mathbf{v}^\epsilon(0, z)=\frac{d}{dt}\left[\mu^\epsilon(t,z)\right]_{t=0}.$$
That is, the initial vorticity determines the time derivative of the Beltrami coefficient at time $t=0$. Thus, it is natural to ask for the dependence of $X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)$ under second-order perturbations of $\mu^\epsilon(t,z)$.
head: environment

label: principal
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: limit
title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{support} we know that $X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)$ is conformal on a neighborhood of $\infty$. Therefore, it has around $\infty$ a Laurent series development whose higher order term is linear,
$$
X^\epsilon(t,z)=a^\epsilon(t)z + b^\epsilon(t)+\frac{c^\epsilon(t)}{z}+...
$$
Also, from Lemma \ref{LinftyK} (b) and the integral representation of $X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)$, we know that
$$\aligned
 |X^\epsilon(t,z)-z| 
&= \left|\int_0^t\operatorname{\textbf{v}}^\epsilon(s,X^\epsilon(s,z))\right| \,ds\\
&\leq \int_0^t \left|\operatorname{\textbf{v}}^\epsilon(s,X^\epsilon(s,z))\right|\,ds\\
&\leq \int_0^tC(K)\,\|\omega^\epsilon(s,\cdot)\|_\infty\,|\operatorname{supp} \omega^\epsilon(s,\cdot)|^\frac12\,ds\\
&\leq \int_0^t C(K)\,\|\omega^\epsilon_0\|_\infty\,|X^\epsilon(s,\operatorname{supp} \omega^\epsilon_0)|^\frac12 \,ds\\
&\leq C(K)\,\|\omega^\epsilon_0\|_\infty \,\int_0^t |X^\epsilon(s,\operatorname{supp} \omega^\epsilon_0)|^\frac12 \,ds\\
&\leq  C(K)\,\|\omega^\epsilon_0\|_\infty\,t\,|\operatorname{supp}\omega^\epsilon_0|^\frac12\,\max_{0\leq s\leq t}\|\det DX^\epsilon(s,\cdot)^\frac12\|_{L^\infty(\operatorname{supp}\omega^\epsilon_0)}.
\endaligned$$
Above, the maximum term on the right hand side  (even depending on $t$ and $\epsilon$) is finite and stays bounded as $|z|\to\infty$, due to the smoothness in $t$ and $z$ of $X^\epsilon(t,z)$. Thus, for every fixed $t$ and $\epsilon>0$ one has
\begin{equation}\label{limit}
\lim_{|z|\to\infty}\frac{|X^\epsilon(t,z)-z|}{|z|}=0.\end{equation}
As a consequence, \eqref{limit} tells us that necessarily $a^\epsilon(t)=1$, and so (a) follows. To see (b), we observe that $X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)-b^\epsilon(t)$ is a  \emph{principal} $\mathcal{K}_t$-quasiconformal map, because 
$$
|X^\epsilon(t,z)-b^\epsilon(t)-z|= O(1/|z|)
$$
as $|z|\to\infty$. Moreover, it is conformal outside of $\operatorname{supp}\omega_0^\epsilon$ by Lemma \ref{support}. Hence, by \cite[Theorem 13.1.2]{AIS}, we have the following area distortion estimates,
$$
|X^\epsilon(t,E)|=|X^\epsilon(t,E)-b^\epsilon(t)|\leq \mathcal{K}_t\,|E|
$$
$\forall E\supset\,\operatorname{supp}(\omega^{\epsilon}_{0})$, as claimed.
head: environment

label: normstability
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Claim (a) can be proved by recalling that $\omega^{\epsilon}(t,\cdot)\circ X^{\epsilon}(t,\cdot) =\omega_0^{\epsilon}(\cdot)$ and the facts that  $X^\epsilon(t,\cdot)$ preserves Lebesgue-null sets and $\|\omega_0^\epsilon\|_\infty\leq\|\omega_0\|_\infty$. 
                                                     
           
                                                    
                                                                         
                                                                                          
   
                                     
                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                             
   
For (b), we use Lemmas \ref{qcflows} (a), \ref{support} and \ref{principal} (b) to obtain
$$
\aligned
\|\omega^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_1
&=\int_{\mathbb C}|\omega^\epsilon(t,z)|\,dA(z)\\
&=\int_{\mathbb C}|\omega^\epsilon_0(\zeta)|\,J^\epsilon(t,\zeta)\,dA(\zeta)\\
&\leq \|\omega^\epsilon_0\|_\infty\,\int_{\operatorname{supp} \omega^\epsilon_0} J^\epsilon(t,\zeta)\,dA(\zeta)\\
&= \|\omega^\epsilon_0\|_\infty\,|X^\epsilon(t,\operatorname{supp} \omega^\epsilon_0)|\\
&\leq \|\omega^\epsilon_0\|_\infty\,\mathcal{K}_t \,|\operatorname{supp}\omega^\epsilon_0|\\
&\leq \|\omega_0\|_\infty\,e^{t\|\omega_0\|_\infty}\,|\operatorname{supp}\omega^\epsilon_0|
\endaligned
$$
as desired.  Estimate (c) follows from Lemma \ref{LinftyK} (b).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
One has
$$
\|\omega^\epsilon(t,\cdot)-\omega(t,\cdot)\|_1\leq
\|\omega_0^\epsilon(X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot))-\omega_0(X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot)\|_1+\|\omega_0 (X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot)-\omega_0(X (-t,\cdot)\|_1
$$
At the first term, we consider a disk $D$ such that $\operatorname{supp}\omega^\epsilon_0,\operatorname{supp}\omega_0\subset D$, and use the higher integrability of quasiconformal jacobians. If $1<p<\frac{\mathcal{K}_t}{\mathcal{K}_t-1}$, 
$$\aligned
\|\omega_0^\epsilon(X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot))-\omega_0(X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot)\|_1
&=\int|\omega_0^\epsilon-\omega_0|\,J^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\\
&\leq\|\omega_0^\epsilon-\omega_0\|_{L^{p'}(D)}\,\|J^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{p}(D)}\\
&\leq\|\omega_0^\epsilon-\omega_0\|_{L^{1}(D)}^\frac1{p'}\,\|\omega_0^\epsilon-\omega_0\|_{L^{\infty}(D)}^\frac1p\,\|J^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{p}(D)}
\endaligned$$
Above, $\|\omega_0^\epsilon-\omega_0\|_{L^{1}(D)}$ converges to $0$, while $\|J^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{p}(D)}$ is bounded in terms of $\mathcal{K}_t$ and $|D|$, 
$$
\aligned
\|J^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{p}(D)}
&=\left(\int_D J^\epsilon(t,\cdot)^{p}\right)^\frac1{p}\\
&\leq C(p, \mathcal{K}_t)\, |D|^{\frac1{p}-1}\int_D J^\epsilon(t,\cdot) \\
&\leq C(p, \mathcal{K}_t)\, |\operatorname{supp}\omega_0^\epsilon|^{\frac1{p} }  \leq C(p, \mathcal{K}_t)\, |\operatorname{supp}\omega_0 |^{\frac1{p} } 
\endaligned
$$
by Lemma \ref{principal} (b) and the reverse H\"older property of quasiconformal jacobians \cite{AIS}, and provided that $\epsilon>0$ is small enough. Concerning the second term, let us choose $\omega_0^n\in C_0$ such that $\|\omega_0^n-\omega_0\|_1\leq 1/n$ and $\|\omega_0^n\|_\infty\leq\|\omega_0\|_\infty$. Then
$$
\aligned
\|\omega_0 (X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot))-\omega_0 (X (-t,\cdot))\|_1
&\leq  \|\omega_0 (X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot))-\omega_0^n(X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot))\|_1\\
&+\|\omega_0^n(X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot))-\omega_0^n(X (-t,\cdot))\|_1\\
&+\|\omega_0^n(X (-t,\cdot))-\omega_0 (X (-t,\cdot))\|_1
\endaligned
$$
Above, again because of the higher integrability of quasiconformal jacobians,
$$\aligned
\|\omega_0(X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot))-\omega_0^n(X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot))\|_1
&=\int  |\omega_0 -\omega_0^n |\,J^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\\
&=\|\omega_0 -\omega_0^n \|_{L^{p'}(D)}\,\|J^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_{L^p(D)}\\
&\leq\|\omega_0 -\omega_0^n \|_{L^{1}(D)}^\frac1{p'}\,\|\omega_0^n-\omega_0\|_\infty^\frac1p\,\|J^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_{L^p(D)}\\
&\leq n^\frac{-1}{p'}\,2^{\frac{1}{p}}\|\omega_0\|_\infty^\frac1p\,\|J^\epsilon(t,\cdot)\|_{L^p(D)}
\endaligned$$
and similarly for $\|\omega_0^n(X (-t,\cdot))-\omega_0(X (-t,\cdot))\|_1$. Thus each of these two terms can be made smaller than $\delta/3$ if $n$ is chosen large enough. The control of the second term comes by continuity. Precisely, as $X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot)\to X(-t,\cdot)$ and $\omega_0^n$ is continuous, there is $\epsilon>0$ such that $\|\omega_0^n(X^\epsilon(-t,\cdot)-\omega_0^n(X(-t,\cdot))\|_\infty<\delta/3$. Thus (a) follows.  For the proof of (b), use (a) and Lemma \ref{LinftyK} (b).
head: environment

label: equivform
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: realimparts
title: Proof
body_md:
We first go from \eqref{vequation}  to \eqref{omegaequation}. We identify $\mathbb R^2\equiv \mathbb C$, and write the system \eqref{vequation} in complex notation,
$$
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{\textbf{v}}_t+\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\,\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}}+\overline\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\,\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}} = -e^{i\theta}\overline{\nabla q}\\-\Delta q = \operatorname{div}(\operatorname{\textbf{v}})\,\operatorname{div}(e^{i\theta}\bar\operatorname{\textbf{v}})\\
\text{Im}(\partial(e^{i\theta}\bar\mathbf{v}))|_{t=0}=0\\
\text{Re}(\partial(e^{i\theta}\bar\operatorname{\textbf{v}}))|_{t=0}=\omega_0\end{cases}
$$
Now, taking $\overline\partial$ on the first equation, and obtain
$$
(\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})_t+\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\,\partial(\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})+\overline\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\,\overline\partial(\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}} )+\overline\partial \operatorname{\textbf{v}} (\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}}+\overline\partial\overline\operatorname{\textbf{v}})= -\overline\partial(e^{i\theta}\overline{\nabla q})
$$
or equivalently,
$$
(\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})_t+\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\cdot\nabla(\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})+ \overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}} \,\operatorname{div}\operatorname{\textbf{v}}= -\frac12\,e^{i\theta}\,\Delta q.
$$
We now multiply by $e^{-i\theta}$, and use the $\mathbb C$-linearity of the transport operator $\frac{d}{dt}+\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\cdot\nabla$ to get
$$
(e^{-i\theta}\,\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})_t+\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\cdot\nabla(e^{-i\theta}\,\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})+ e^{-i\theta}\,\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}} \,\operatorname{div}\operatorname{\textbf{v}}= -\frac12\,\Delta q.
$$
After taking real and imaginary parts, 
\begin{equation}\label{realimparts}
\begin{cases}
\text{Re} ((e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})_t+\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\cdot\nabla(e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}}))+\text{Re}(e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})\,\operatorname{div}\operatorname{\textbf{v}} = -\frac12\,\Delta q\\
\text{Im}((e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})_t+\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\cdot\nabla(e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}}))+\text{Im}(e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})\,\operatorname{div}\operatorname{\textbf{v}}= 0.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
The above equations may be seen as scalar conservation laws for $\text{Re}(e^{-i\theta}\,\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})$ and $\text{Im}(e^{-i\theta}\,\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})$. The second one is homogeneous, and so from the initial condition
$$2\,\text{Im}(e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})|_{t=0}=-\operatorname{curl}(\mathbf M_\theta\operatorname{\textbf{v}})|_{t=0}=0$$ 
we deduce that at any time $t>0$  
$$2\,\text{Im}(e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})=-\operatorname{curl}(\mathbf M_\theta\operatorname{\textbf{v}})=0.$$ 
To see this, simply call $\rho=2\,\text{Im}(e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})$ and note it satisfies the following initial value problem, 
$$\begin{cases}
\frac{d}{dt}\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho\,\operatorname{\textbf{v}})=0\\\rho(0,\cdot)=0
\end{cases}$$
which has $\rho=0$ as its unique solution, due to the smoothness of $\operatorname{\textbf{v}}$. As a consequence, $e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\in\mathbb R$ and so if we now denote $\omega=2\text{Re}(e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})$, then 
$$\omega = \operatorname{div}(e^{i\theta}\bar\operatorname{\textbf{v}}).$$ 
Thus the first equation at \eqref{realimparts} implies that 
$$\omega_t+\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\cdot\nabla\omega+\omega\,\operatorname{div}\operatorname{\textbf{v}}= -\Delta q.$$
Now, since the second equation at \eqref{vequation} tells us that $\omega\,\operatorname{div}\operatorname{\textbf{v}}= -\Delta q$, we necessarily have for $\omega$ a homogeneous transport equation
$$\omega_t+\operatorname{\textbf{v}}\cdot\nabla\omega=0$$
together with the initial condition $\omega|_{t=0}=\operatorname{div}(e^{i\theta}\bar\operatorname{\textbf{v}})|_{t=0}=\omega_0$ as claimed. \\
\\
For the converse implication, we start by noting that our choice of the kernel $K$ and the second equation in \eqref{omegaequation} tell  us that $2e^{-i\theta}\overline\partial\mathbf{v}=\omega$, which by assumption is real valued. We now use the first equation in \eqref{omegaequation}, together with the $\mathbb C$-linearity of the complex operator, to get
$$
\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}}_t + \operatorname{\textbf{v}}\cdot\partial(\overline\partial \operatorname{\textbf{v}})+\overline{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}}\cdot\overline\partial(\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})=0
$$
or equivalently
$$
\overline\partial(\operatorname{\textbf{v}}_t +  \operatorname{\textbf{v}} \cdot\partial \operatorname{\textbf{v}}+\overline{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}}\cdot\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}})=  \overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}} \,\operatorname{div}\operatorname{\textbf{v}}
$$
We now complex conjugate at both sides of the equality, multiply by $e^{i\theta}$, and use $\mathbb C$-linearity of the transport operator, and obtain
\begin{equation}\label{aqui}
\partial(e^{i\theta}(\overline{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}_t +  \operatorname{\textbf{v}} \cdot\partial \operatorname{\textbf{v}}+\overline{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}}\cdot\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}}}))=\frac\omega2\,\operatorname{div}\operatorname{\textbf{v}}
\end{equation}
By assumption, the right hand side above is real, whence $e^{i\theta}(\overline{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}_t +  \operatorname{\textbf{v}} \cdot\partial \operatorname{\textbf{v}}+\overline{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}}\cdot\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}}})$ is a conservative vector field. Thus there exists a scalar valued potential $q$ such that
$$
e^{i\theta}(\overline{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}_t +  \operatorname{\textbf{v}} \cdot\partial \operatorname{\textbf{v}}+\overline{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}}\cdot\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}}})=-\nabla q
$$ 
This automatically gives the first equation at \eqref{vequation}. Moreover, if we take real parts at \eqref{aqui},
$$-\frac12\Delta q=\frac12\operatorname{div}(e^{i\theta}(\overline{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}_t +  \operatorname{\textbf{v}} \cdot\partial \operatorname{\textbf{v}}+\overline{\operatorname{\textbf{v}}}\cdot\overline\partial\operatorname{\textbf{v}}}))=\frac\omega2\,\operatorname{div}\operatorname{\textbf{v}}$$
or equivalently
$$-\Delta q= \operatorname{div}(\operatorname{\textbf{v}})\,\operatorname{div}(\mathbf M_\theta \operatorname{\textbf{v}})$$
as claimed. The third and fourth equations in \eqref{vequation} are automatic from the second and fourth in \eqref{omegaequation}.
